blocks.md: **On April 1, 1992 New Jersey raised its minimum wage from \$4.25 to \$5.05 (+18.8%), while Pennsylvania stayed at \$4.25. Surveying 410 Burger King, KFC, Wendy's and Roy Rogers restaurants a month before and eight months after, Card and Krueger found full-time-equivalent employment per store rose slightly in New Jersey relative to Pennsylvania (+2.76), along with starting wages and meal prices.**

blocks.src: assets/Attachments/Card and Krueger 1994 - distribution of starting wages in NJ and PA.png
blocks.alt: Card and Krueger 1994 - distribution of starting wages in NJ and PA
blocks.caption: Starting wages piled up at \$4.25 in both states in February 1992; by November 85% of New Jersey stores paid exactly \$5.05.

blocks.src: assets/Attachments/Table - Card and Krueger 1994 average employment per store.png
blocks.alt: Table - Card and Krueger 1994 average employment per store

blocks.md: Within New Jersey, low-wage stores (most affected) gained 3.36 FTE relative to high-wage stores, which the increase did not touch.

| Dependent variable | NJ dummy | Initial wage gap |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Change in FTE employment, no controls | 2.33 (1.19) | 15.65 (6.08) |
| … with chain and ownership controls | 2.30 (1.20) | 14.92 (6.21) |
| Change in log meal price, with controls | 0.037 (0.014) | 0.146 (0.074) |
The wage gap is $GAP_i = (5.05 - W_{1i})/W_{1i}$ for New Jersey stores below \$5.05 and 0 otherwise; it predicts the actual proportional wage change well ($R^2 = 0.75$).

sections.heading: Reanalysis with administrative data (Card and Krueger 2000)

blocks.md: With BLS ES-202 payroll records for the same chains ([Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW)](note:quarterly-census-of-employment-and-wages-qcew)), the New Jersey–Pennsylvania employment differential is small and insignificant: 0.225 (1.029) in levels with controls, 0.009 (0.029) proportionally. Over 1991–1997, the 1996 federal increase bound in Pennsylvania but not New Jersey, and again employment moved together.
